#### Writing Regular Expressions

Assume that the vocabulary is `{a, b}`. Give regular expressions for the following languages:

1. All sequences that contain `aa` and `bb`.

`(a|b)* (aa (a|b)* bb | bb (a|b)* aa) (a|b)*`

Either `aa` comes before `bb` (`...aa...bb...`) or `bb` comes before `aa` (`...bb...aa...`). The two halves of the disjunction cover both possible orderings of the two required substrings.

2. All sequences that do not begin with `aaa`.

$\varepsilon | a | aa | b(a|b)^* | ab(a|b)^* | aab(a|b)^*$

A string fails to begin with `aaa` iff one of:
- it is empty, `a`, or `aa` (too short to contain `aaa` at the front), or
- its first character is `b` (case `b(a|b)*`), or
- it begins with `a` but its second character is `b` (case `ab(a|b)*`), or
- it begins with `aa` but its third character is `b` (case `aab(a|b)*`).

Equivalent, factored form using a single optional prefix of `a`s:

$(\varepsilon | a | aa) (\varepsilon | b (a|b)^*)$

The first factor matches any prefix of 0, 1, or 2 `a`s; the second factor either stops there or continues with a `b` and any tail. This guarantees that after at most two `a`s the string either ends or has a non-`a`, so it never starts with `aaa`.

3. All sequences in which `aa` occurs exactly once. Note that in `aaa`, the sequence `aa` occurs twice.

`(b | ab)* aa (b | ba)*`

The first factor matches any prefix of 0, 1, or 2 `a`s; the second factor either stops there or continues with a `b` and any tail. This guarantees that after at most two `a`s the string either ends or has a non-`a`, so it never starts with `aaa`.

3. All sequences in which `aa` occurs exactly once. Note that in `aaa`, the sequence `aa` occurs twice.

`(b | ab)* aa (b | ba)*`

Read left-to-right: before the `aa`, every maximal run of `a`s must have length at most 1, so the prefix is built from `b`-or-`ab` chunks (each contributes at most one `a` and that `a` is followed by `b`). After the `aa`, the same constraint holds in mirror image: every run of `a`s has length at most 1 and is preceded by `b` (so the tail is `b`-or-`ba` chunks). The `aa` in the middle is therefore the unique pair of consecutive `a`s; nowhere else in the string can two `a`s be adjacent.

Note `aaa` is excluded because the third `a` would create a second occurrence (`aa` starting at position 0 *and* at position 1).

4. All sequences in which every `a` is either immediately preceded or immediately followed by a `b`, for example, `baab`, `aba`, `b`.

$\varepsilon | (b | ab)(b | ab | aab)^* (\varepsilon | a)$

The structure: think of the string as built from the chunks `b`, `ab`, `aab`, with an optional trailing `a` (giving `…ba` at the end).

4. All sequences in which every `a` is either immediately preceded or immediately followed by a `b`, for example, `baab`, `aba`, `b`.

$\varepsilon | (b | ab)(b | ab | aab)^* (\varepsilon | a)$

The structure: think of the string as built from the chunks `b`, `ab`, `aab`, with an optional trailing `a` (giving `…ba` at the end).

- Inside the middle `(b|ab|aab)*` every `a` is paired with a `b` to its right (in `ab`) or surrounded by `b`s (in `aab` — the second `a` of `aab` is between two characters: the first `a` on its left and the `b` on its right; the first `a` is preceded by whatever came before, which must end in `b`, and followed by another `a`, so its only required `b`-neighbor is on the right after the next `a`. Actually `aab` lets a *pair* of adjacent `a`s sit between two `b`s.)
- The start `(b | ab)` ensures no string begins with a bare `a` whose only neighbor is another `a`.
- The tail $(\varepsilon | a)$ permits a final `a` whose left neighbor (the last char of the previous chunk) is necessarily `b`.

Examples in the language: $\varepsilon$, `b`, `bb`, `ab`, `ba`, `bab`, `aba`, `baab`, `ababab`, `babab`.

Examples rejected: `a` (no `b`-neighbor), `aa`, `aab` (the first `a` has no `b`-neighbor), `aaa`, `baa` (last `a` has only `a` to its left and end-of-string to its right), `aabb` (same reason).
